# Auve Tech’s Driverless Shuttle Playbook for Airports and Beyond

**From:** The AV Market Strategist <avmarketstrategist@substack.com>  
**Date:** 2026-10-22T17:00:39.000Z

---

View this post on the web at https://avmarketstrategist.substack.com/p/auve-techs-driverless-shuttle-playbook

Robotaxis get the billions. But driverless shuttles on airports and private campuses may scale first, because the owner of the ground can say yes before the law changes.
Taavi Rõivas was Prime Minister of Estonia. Today he chairs Auve Tech, a Tallinn company that designs its own eight-seat shuttle, MiCa, and its own self-driving software. Its shuttles run in small Japanese towns, in West Palm Beach and Abu Dhabi, and on the airside of Tallinn Airport with nobody on board.
First, the bet. I asked why Auve Tech chose low-speed shuttles when most of the money chased robotaxis, why Navya and EasyMile struggled, and why a company this size builds the vehicle and the software instead of picking one. Taavi explains the redundancy behind MiCa and how a new route goes from 3D map to driverless.
Then the economics. A driverless shuttle costs more than a minivan, so the saving has to come from the driver. Taavi explains how many vehicles one remote operator must monitor before the numbers flip, why that ratio differs between Switzerland and Dubai, and why the driver shortage at airports matters as much as cost.
Then the deployments: what the regulator needed to see before the safety operator could leave the vehicle at Tallinn Airport, why the customer there also sends tools and aircraft parts on their own, and what daily rides with elderly passengers in Japan show about acceptance.
It ends with the Middle East, Chinese robobuses arriving in Europe, whether “made in Europe” really sells, and the one rule a former head of government would change to scale driverless shuttles.
